title: Magic: The Gathering Arena
review_text: TL;DR: Magic: The Gathering Arena is the most generous, fun, and accessible digital card game for casual players—easily beating Hearthstone’s brutal economy and Yu-Gi-Oh’s endless combo turns, despite minor display bugs on ultrawide monitors. A Casual Player’s Perspective on MTG Arena I’m not entirely sure how many total hours I’ve put into MTG Arena between Steam and mobile, but I’d estimate around 30 to 40 hours. For context, I come from a solid card game background: around 300 hours in Hearthstone, roughly 50 hours in modern Yu-Gi-Oh!, and over 300 hours as a legacy Yu-Gi-Oh! player. I originally ran a purely free-to-play account before starting fresh with a new account where I’ve spent maybe $20 to $30 total over the years. I mostly play on my phone, so keep in mind: I’m a casual mobile player who rarely spends money. Here is my honest experience. Economy and Progression: Genuinely Free-to-Play Friendly When I first started years ago, I did some research, built a meta deck within my first week, and maintained roughly a 70% win rate once I learned the ropes. Even after completing that first deck, I had nearly enough leftover wildcards to build a second one—I was only short a couple of mythics. On my current account, the game has been ridiculously generous: Massive Resource Pool: I currently have over 5,000 gold and dozens of wildcards (including over 10 mythic, 24 rare, and 50 common wildcards). That’s more than enough to craft two top-tier meta decks right now. Passive Pack Acquisition: Just by playing casually without spending cash, I’ve opened around 20 packs from the latest set. Zero Pay Pressure: I have never once felt starved for cards or pressured to open my wallet. Ironically, I’ve spent the last 30 hours playing completely unedited Starter/Standard decks. Did I lose a lot? Absolutely. But winning wasn't the goal—learning and having fun was. I haven’t even bothered crafting a new meta deck yet because I enjoy the core gameplay loop too much to rush it. I also love the crossover sets (Universes Beyond). I know that’s a divisive topic in the community, but the gameplay interactions are wild. In one match, an opponent forced me to discard my entire hand and pinged me for 5 life every time I played a card. I thought I had the win locked down when they were at 8 life, only to bleed out and lose completely. It was hilarious, unique, and easily the most fun match I’ve had in ages. How It Stacks Up Against the Competition Hearthstone Hearthstone has become an exhausting money pit. Ranked mode is overrun with bots. Card sets become irrelevant remarkably fast. Keeping up with Standard feels like it demands $150 every three months. In Magic, the 2-year Standard rotation window gives cards real longevity. Casual play easily keeps pace with the format. The disenchant/dust economy in Hearthstone is terrible. I spent hundreds of dollars on that game over the years, and after stepping away for a while, every single card I bought became useless in Standard. I returned to zero wildcards, minimal dust value, and only cosmetic items left to show for it. Combine that with high-RNG gameplay, and it simply wasn't worth staying. Yu-Gi-Oh! Yu-Gi-Oh! is actually quite welcoming and generous with its card acquisition—much like MTG. The new player experience was smooth, and getting cards for a ranked deck didn’t require cash. The problem is the modern match pacing. The game revolves heavily around One-Turn Kills (OTKs). Too many matches feel like watching someone assemble a massive solitary puzzle on turn two while you wait ten minutes to find out if you're allowed to play. It's a great game, but that specific playstyle just isn't for me. The Big Flaw: Ultrawide Support My main technical complaint is Arena’s poor Ultrawide (UWHD) implementation on PC. On a 3440×1440 ultrawide monitor, the client fails to hold its aspect ratio in fullscreen, frequently glitching or stretching when navigating between menus. I have to force a standard 16:9 window just to keep the interface stable. It isn't game-breaking, but it feels like lazy display coding for a studio this size. Final Verdict: 8/10 The game has a steep initial learning curve, optimal pack acquisition requires external research, and the PC client has technical oversights like broken ultrawide scaling. However, if you're a casual player looking for a rewarding, deep card game where you can build competitive decks without being nickel-and-dimed, MTG Arena is easily the best option on the market.

review_text: It's digital MtG, so if you like to play the game but don't want to haul or sort your collection this is for you. Let's talk monetization, because that is the worst part of any game like this. But the thing is, free-to-play in this game DOES NOT mean pay-to-win. You can spend stupid amounts of money on your collection if that's your thing, but you really don't need to spend a dime. Season passes? Yes, those are here, but you can actually earn the gems to unlock them through free play. You earn gold through daily quests (easily earned through starter deck duels, so you're never at a wealth disadvantage) and then you can spend that gold to enter draft competitions to win gems. The conversion rates will depend on your win rate, but you can absolutely EARN the premium currency rather than paying real money. There are more play modes than I can even count with events and opportunities constantly shifting. Some of them (constructed and historic, mainly) will be full of players with the strongest decks that money can buy, and anyone who hasn't made that kind of investment is going to lose a LOT. Still, even on your first day you'll likely have enough wildcards to build *one* such deck--but after that you'll need to pay for more wildcards or earn them very slowly before you'll have enough to build another.

title: Mycopunk
review_text: Fixes virtually every issue I have with other similar games while feeling distinctly like its own thing. Every other looter shooter I've played is very concerned about not letting the player have too much power. Not the case here. There's not a massive abundance of guns like destiny or borderlands, but there's a good variety of weapons that handle distinctly. The weapon mod system also allows you to pretty drastically alter how they feel. I also am compelled to theory craft and find new ways to break the game because (unlike destiny) the devs aren't deciding which build will be the best for the current patch. This is genuinely the first looter shooter I've played to deliver on the promise of "diablo with guns." There is many ways to make an OP character without chasing some kind of meta. It side steps a lot of the grindy feeling that other games in the genre have because it's not particularly picky about how you progress. The mission objectives are very much in the vein of something like deep rock or helldivers but the game doesn't push you too hard to play one type of mission over another. Grinding the mission chain things in deep rock just to get an unlock that felt mediocre sapped any and all energy I had to play that game after a while. The backlog system in this game allows you to give yourself that kind of structure if you crave it, but you ultimately have control over what you choose to do. You progress by getting mods for your gear and all of the activities give you mods for your gear. A thing I've come to really despise in all of these post left 4 dead co op shooters is the rigid class systems. I constantly feel like I'm being forced to give up some invaluable piece of kit in order to fit some kind of team composition. In practice if you're playing with randoms it makes it harder to step up and cover areas they may be lacking in, and it also usually makes solo play pretty miserable. This one being class based nearly put me off of it, but I actually like what they did here. The weapons are not class locked which instantly makes the whole system way more tolerable. You don't have to play the cowboy character to have a revolver. The class abilities don't fit neatly into archetypes either. You can build them to fulfill whatever type of role you want. It plays well solo too. The enemies are pretty interesting. They didn't just copy paste the specials from left 4 dead. There's definitely enemy types, but there's a lot less emphasis placed on this than you're probably used to. The enemies are modular and when you kill one the parts they dropped can be picked up and used to attack you by other enemies. I thought it was really easy for the first few missions as I was unlocking the higher difficulties, but it's not balanced around the difficulty of the individual enemies. This game has helldivers style hordes that feel very chaotic and alive when you're fighting them. The difficulty comes from trying to manage the horde. That always feels different because your objectives change depending on the mission, and the makeup of the horde its self changes as you fight it. It's really pretty unique and works extremely well with this games systems. You'll get more powerful and you will have the power fantasy/diablo style moments of making your whole screen explode, but the game never becomes a cakewalk. I don't like roguelikes, but this game also has an excellent roguelike mode. It gives you a fresh character and gives you new mods after every encounter. It gets progressively harder and there's modifiers. It's typical roguelike stuff. All of the systems the game is built on are so well put together that I actually had a ton of fun playing it though. It feels like previewing what types of builds I can make in the other parts of the game, in addition to stress testing whatever I come up with on the fly. It also gives you a way to unlock the mods that you got in the roguelike mode for your main characters, so its a really solid way to progress overall. It runs great. Art style isn't for everyone. I thought it looked kind of ugly in videos but it grew on me while I played. The music is good. Shooting things feels good. Tone is comedic, but it's pretty lightly implemented and not an overbearing assault on the senses like borderlands. There's a good hub for when you're between missions. It doesn't inundate you with tutorials. Everything feels good. I can't believe I had never heard of this prior to its full release on my steam release calendar thingy. It's also absolutely absurd that you can't find a youtube video on it from less than 10 months ago. At the time of writing there's 1 video on it from a day ago and it's AI generated. This feels like the kind of thing that should be way bigger than it is. All in all, this is the first game of it's type that doesn't feel like it's constantly trying to hold me back from the fun part. 15 bucks is generous and 7 is highway robbery. Highly recommend.

review_text: Game runs worse and worse with each update. There is nothing to do most of the time and stuff you could do is basically capped either weekly or daily. It takes 3 Minutes to spend every pixel (the daily currency) and about 30min-1h to spend the weekly stuff. The fights were nice at first but they have become a chore. The game lacks supports, they lack to the point that every team needs character A in its composition and when you do the "endgame" stuff, you need TWO teams and one character cannot be in two teams at once. Every new character aside from one, have been on field dps (which is 8 in total) and one can be argued to be an off field dps with support capability. Building your teams also takes extremely long, since the weekly material is limited too and you need 30+ for ONE character, meaning you spend like half a year on one team. The non 50/50 is a godsend though and should be adapted by other gacha games. The story is great. The fight system is fun (if it works correctly and doesnt eat every input imaginable, which it sadly does a lot). Driving around the city got worse and worse, the game started lagging, not badly but it did get worse. If it wasnt for the power creep and the lack of support characters, id probably say, go for it but as it is right now, i would not recommend it.
